lesson: Point One — give the point a body (chapter 1, second lesson; Godot 4.6, GDScript)
purpose: Atomic claims of the uncompressed lesson, written before compression, so loss can be measured after a compress-unfold round trip.

kinds.code: a specific code element or line that must be there
kinds.direction: the direction of a thought: why this comes next, what it leads to, what question it opens
kinds.force: how strongly or under what condition a claim holds
kinds.connection: the link between a shortcut and the system it must enter

claims.text: The lesson's aim, stated in its title, is to give the point a body.
The lesson builds on Point Zero, which gave an instruction (_ready()) that runs when the scene is ready.
This lesson uses that ready moment to place a marker.
The supplied scene already gives a floor, a light and a view (camera); the student does not build them.
The floor, light and view are kept; only what appears in front of the viewer is changed.
Open the Point One study project (doc/book/studies/point-one/README.md), then open study.tscn.
The root node of study.tscn is PointStudy.
There are three station nodes: Position, Visible and Solid.
position.gd is attached to Position, visible.gd to Visible, solid.gd to Solid.
These three scripts are the ones the student will change; nothing else in the study is edited.
Each station has its own “Point one” label.
Run the study.
Above the first label there is nothing; above the next two labels are white spheres.
Three small pink feelers move from left to right, one through each station.
Two feelers cross their stations; the third stops at the solid sphere.
The sweep repeats.
Space pauses or resumes the sweep; R starts the sweep again.
contact_probe.gd supplies the contact test (the feelers).
The feelers' movement is borrowed equipment, like the camera: supplied, not built or edited in this lesson.
The lesson will change what the feeler can cross, not how it moves.
Open position.gd.
The three lines shown are the whole of position.gd; nothing else is in it.
Each of the three station scripts begins with `extends Node3D`.
Each script's construction sits inside `func _ready() -> void:`.
position.gd's only statement is `var point_position := Vector3(0.0, 1.12, 0.0)`.
_ready() is the function already known from Point Zero.
`-> void` says the function returns no value.
A Vector3 is a value containing three numbers.
The line defines a Vector3 and names it point_position.
For now, point_position is simply the supplied position at the station; its three components are not yet studied.
Point Coordinates, a later lesson, will make the Vector3's three components its subject.
In position.gd change 1.12 to 1.7 and run.
Nothing appears at the Position station after that change.
The change altered a value without attaching a visible body to it: a value alone shows nothing.
The editor's unused-variable warning describes that condition (point_position is defined but nothing uses it).
The pink feeler still crosses the empty place at the first station.
The feeler belongs to the supplied test, not to the position just defined; changing point_position does not affect it.
Restore 1.12 in position.gd.
Open visible.gd.
The complete construction in visible.gd runs inside the same familiar _ready() function.
visible.gd starts with the same `var point_position := Vector3(0.0, 1.12, 0.0)`.
`var radius := 0.14`
`var sphere := SphereMesh.new()`
`sphere.radius = radius`
`sphere.height = radius * 2.0`
`var marker := MeshInstance3D.new()`
`marker.mesh = sphere`
`marker.position = point_position`
`add_child(marker)`
point_position is the location.
sphere (a SphereMesh) describes a spherical surface.
marker (a MeshInstance3D) is the node that displays that surface.
`.new()` creates each part.
Assigning marker.mesh gives that node its surface.
Assigning marker.position places the node.
add_child(marker) joins the marker to the station.
A position and the object placed there are different things.
In visible.gd change 1.12 to 1.7 and run.
The white sphere rises: the middle number, 1.12, is the height.
Restore the height, then change radius from 0.14 to 0.3.
The sphere grows around the same centre.
The sphere's height follows the radius only because the script makes the height twice the radius.
Watch the feeler cross the larger sphere.
A visible surface, however large, still gives the feeler nothing to collide with.
How much the sphere hides can be changed without changing what can pass through it.
Restore the radius to 0.14.
The third station looks the same as the second, but its feeler stops.
Open solid.gd.
solid.gd's first part repeats visible.gd's marker construction unchanged (point_position, radius, sphere, marker, add_child(marker)).
`var solid := StaticBody3D.new()`
`solid.position = point_position`
`var sphere_shape := SphereShape3D.new()`
`sphere_shape.radius = radius`
`var collider := CollisionShape3D.new()`
`collider.shape = sphere_shape`
`solid.add_child(collider)`: the collider is a child of the body, not of the station.
`add_child(solid)`: the body is joined to the station.
A StaticBody3D participates in collision.
SphereShape3D describes the body's boundary.
CollisionShape3D attaches that shape to the physics body.
The visible marker and the body are both placed at point_position.
The one radius value feeds both the visible sphere (sphere.radius) and the boundary (sphere_shape.radius), so surface and boundary match until one line is changed.
Find `sphere_shape.radius = radius` and change it to `sphere_shape.radius = 0.35`.
Change only that one line: the visible radius stays 0.14.
Run again.
The white sphere stays small, but the feeler stops earlier, leaving a visible gap.
The empty space between surface and boundary resists the feeler.
Debug → Visible Collision Shapes can reveal the larger boundary.
The contact test works without that overlay; the overlay is optional.
The student has chosen whether the surface we see and the boundary we encounter coincide.
In the museum, it is the visitor's own movement that meets this difference between surface and boundary.
The fixed-camera study supplies another moving body (the feeler) so the same relation can be tested.
Restore `sphere_shape.radius = radius`.
Try a different disagreement: in solid.gd set the visible radius to 0.3 and sphere_shape.radius to 0.07.
The feeler disappears into the white surface before the contact label reports “stopped”.
A contact label reports “stopped” when a feeler meets a boundary.
The boundary is now inside the body we see.
When finished, return both radii to the matching 0.14.
The light can be removed while the body is kept (section title “Remove the light, keep the body”): what lights a body is separate from the body.
In the museum, use the wall switch.
The long shadows disappear while a dim fill leaves the spheres visible.
The collision boundary stays where it was when the light goes off.
The switch's decision is one line: `sun.visible = false`.
sun is the museum's directional light.
`sun.visible = false` is a reading of the museum source, not a line to paste into visible.gd.
visible.gd has no variable named sun.
The portable study keeps its supplied light; the switch exists only in the museum.
Building the switch and its lighting rig is outside this lesson.
The student can now place a marker, change its surface around the same centre, and give it a different physical boundary.
The large sphere at the end of the museum corridor still says “Point one”.
That sphere asks the student to return to those three choices.
Knowing its construction gives the student another way to change the encounter.
Point Coordinates begins with a supplied point the student can hold, then reads its movement.
Point Coordinates will prepare two positions for the line.
The construction reference (doc/book/studies/point-one/CONSTRUCTION.md) keeps the roles of the supplied parts available.
The construction reference adds no required exercise.
Every experiment ends by restoring what it changed (1.12, radius 0.14, sphere_shape.radius = radius), so the next starts from the matching default.
The three stations run in order, each adding one layer to the same position: a value only, then a surface, then a boundary.

quiz.q: What is a Vector3, and what is the Vector3 in position.gd called?
quiz.answer: A value containing three numbers; it is named point_position, defined as Vector3(0.0, 1.12, 0.0).

quiz.q: You change 1.12 to 1.7 in position.gd and run. What appears at that station, and what does the editor tell you?
quiz.answer: Nothing appears: a value was changed without attaching a visible body to it. The editor's unused-variable warning describes that condition.

quiz.q: Why does the first feeler still cross the empty station after you change point_position?
quiz.answer: The feeler belongs to the supplied contact test (contact_probe.gd), not to the position you defined; its movement is borrowed equipment, like the camera.

quiz.q: In visible.gd, which two parts are made with .new(), and which three lines give the marker its surface, its place and its parent?
quiz.answer: A SphereMesh (sphere, the spherical surface) and a MeshInstance3D (marker, the node that displays it). marker.mesh = sphere gives the surface, marker.position = point_position places it, add_child(marker) joins it to the station.

quiz.q: You change radius from 0.14 to 0.3 in visible.gd. What happens to the sphere's size and centre, and why does its height change too?
quiz.answer: It grows around the same centre. The height follows only because the script sets sphere.height = radius * 2.0.

quiz.q: Does a larger visible sphere stop the feeler at the second station?
quiz.answer: No. A visible surface, however large, gives the feeler nothing to collide with; you can change how much the sphere hides without changing what can pass through it.

quiz.q: Which three classes does solid.gd add so the feeler stops, what does each do, and how are they parented?
quiz.answer: StaticBody3D participates in collision; SphereShape3D describes its boundary; CollisionShape3D attaches that shape to the body. The collider is added to the body (solid.add_child(collider)), and the body to the station (add_child(solid)).

quiz.q: Why do the white sphere and its boundary coincide in solid.gd as supplied?
quiz.answer: Both are placed at point_position, and both are sized from the same radius variable (sphere.radius = radius and sphere_shape.radius = radius).

quiz.q: You change only sphere_shape.radius to 0.35 and run. What do you see, and do you need the Debug overlay to know it?
quiz.answer: The white sphere stays small but the feeler stops earlier, leaving a visible gap: the empty space resists it. Debug → Visible Collision Shapes can show the larger boundary, but the contact test works without it.

quiz.q: Visible radius 0.3, sphere_shape.radius 0.07: what happens, and what do you do afterwards?
quiz.answer: The feeler disappears into the white surface before the contact label reports “stopped”: the boundary is inside the visible body. Afterwards return both to the matching 0.14.

quiz.q: In the museum there is no feeler. What meets the surface/boundary difference there, why does the study supply a feeler, and which part of the feeler do you change?
quiz.answer: Your own movement meets it in the museum. The fixed-camera study supplies the feeler as another moving body to test the same relation. Its movement is borrowed equipment you do not change; you change only what it can cross, by choosing whether surface and boundary coincide. No overlay is needed to see the result.

quiz.q: Can you paste `sun.visible = false` into visible.gd? What does the museum switch change, and what stays?
quiz.answer: No: it is a reading of the museum source, sun is the museum's directional light, and visible.gd has no variable named sun. The switch removes the long shadows while a dim fill keeps the spheres visible; the collision boundary stays where it was. The study keeps its supplied light, and building the switch is outside this lesson. The light can go while the body stays.

quiz.q: What does this lesson leave open about point_position, and what will Point Coordinates do next?
quiz.answer: For now point_position is just the supplied position; its three components are not studied. Point Coordinates makes those components its subject: it begins with a supplied point you can hold, reads its movement, and prepares two positions for the line.

quiz.q: What in the museum asks you to return to this lesson's choices, and must you work through the construction reference?
quiz.answer: The large sphere at the end of the museum corridor, which still says “Point one”; knowing its construction gives another way to change the encounter. The construction reference keeps the roles of the supplied parts available but adds no required exercise.

quiz.q: What is the root of study.tscn, which script belongs to which station, and which keys control the sweep?
quiz.answer: The root is PointStudy. Position has position.gd, Visible has visible.gd, Solid has solid.gd. Space pauses or resumes the sweep; R starts it again.

quiz.q: Why does the lesson run from nothing, to a surface, to a boundary, and what distinction does that order teach?
quiz.answer: Each station adds one layer to the same position, giving the point a body step by step. It teaches that a position and the object placed there are different things, and that you choose whether the surface you see and the boundary you meet coincide. Each experiment is restored so the next starts from the matching default.
